youtube.title: Why Are Ships Afraid of Bab el-Mandeb?
youtube.description:
Every ship that sails the Red Sea between the Suez Canal and Asia must pass one narrow gap at its southern end: the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Why did so many ships start to avoid it after 2023, and can the world really go around it?

We follow the strait on the map: its two channels, the empires that took its shores, the headland still argued over, the foreign bases in Djibouti, the Red Sea attacks and the warships that answered, and the three roads that could redraw the map from here, with each side's case.

{CHAPTERS}

youtube.comment: Which narrow strait should we map next? 👇

sources.claim: The strait is about 29 kilometres (18 miles) wide at its narrowest
sources.source: US Energy Information Administration, World Oil Transit Chokepoints (2019, updated 2024)

sources.claim: Britannica gives about 32 kilometres
From late 2023, many ships turned away and sailed around Africa
sources.source: Reuters, December 2023 (Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd advisories); Suez Canal Authority transit figures via Reuters, January 2025

sources.claim: Perim splits it into an eastern channel about 3 km wide and 30 m deep, and a western one about 26 km wide and 310 m deep
Perim is about 13 square kilometres and belongs to Yemen
The Red Sea runs about 1,930 kilometres from Suez to the strait
The Suez Canal opened in 1869
Ships use two traffic lanes, one each way, separated by a buffer
In 2023, nearly nine million barrels (8.7 million) of oil a day passed the strait; about 4 million in 2024
sources.source: EIA, Today in Energy, Red Sea chokepoint oil flows (2025)

sources.claim: About 26,400 ships crossed Suez in 2023 and about 13,200 in 2024
sources.source: Suez Canal Authority figures, reported by Reuters and Ahram Online, January 2025

sources.claim: More than 70 ships a day in 2023
Yemen divided by civil war since 2014, when the Houthis, a movement from the north, took Sanaa
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Yemen Civil War'; Reuters, September 2014

sources.claim: The Houthis hold Sanaa and Hodeidah
sources.source: UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, final report 2024

sources.claim: Government-allied forces hold the coast beside the strait, including Mocha
sources.source: Reuters, February 2017 (Mocha retaken); UN Panel of Experts 2024

sources.claim: British forces captured Aden in January 1839, as a coaling station on the route to India
Aden is about 170 kilometres east of the strait
sources.source: Great-circle measure between Aden (12.8N 45.0E) and the strait (12.6N 43.4E)

sources.claim: Britain took Perim in 1857
France signed a treaty with Afar rulers for Obock in 1862
In 1869 an Italian shipping company (Rubattino) bought land at Assab; Italy proclaimed Eritrea a colony in 1890
By 1890 France held the southern shore (Djibouti founded 1888)
The canal put the strait on the main sea road between Europe and Asia
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Bab el-Mandeb Strait' (importance grew with the Suez Canal)

sources.claim: Britain left Aden in November 1967; Perim went to South Yemen
Djibouti became independent in June 1977
Eritrea became independent from Ethiopia in 1993
Ethiopia has about 130 million people, the most populous landlocked country
Eritrea and Yemen fought over the Hanish Islands in December 1995
sources.source: Permanent Court of Arbitration, Eritrea/Yemen case records

sources.claim: The 1998 award gave most islands to Yemen; the 1999 award drew the sea border roughly along a median line, adjusted around islands
sources.source: Permanent Court of Arbitration, Awards of 9 October 1998 and 17 December 1999

sources.claim: Djibouti and Eritrea both claim Ras Doumeira; clash June 2008; Qatar withdrew its peacekeepers in 2017
Ras Doumeira is still disputed and the border there is unmarked
sources.source: UN Security Council resolution 1862 (14 January 2009); Reuters, June 2017

sources.claim: Djibouti has about a million people and hosts US, French, Chinese, Japanese and Italian bases
sources.source: World Bank 2024 (about 1.1 million); US Congressional Research Service, 'Djibouti' (2023)

sources.claim: The US pays about 63 million dollars a year for Camp Lemonnier under a 2014 deal
China opened its first overseas military base in Djibouti in August 2017, about 12 km from Camp Lemonnier
sources.source: Reuters / Xinhua, 1 August 2017; distance measured between published coordinates (published figures about 12-13 km)

sources.claim: In October 1973, Egypt's navy blockaded the strait to Israel-bound ships; no border changed
sources.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Yom Kippur War'; The New York Times, October 1973

sources.claim: Houthi forces seized the Galaxy Leader on 19 November 2023 in the southern Red Sea
The Houthis said they acted over the Gaza war, targeting ships linked to Israel, later the US and Britain
sources.source: Houthi statements reported by Reuters, November 2023 and January 2024

sources.claim: Gaza is about 2,000 kilometres north of Sanaa
More than 100 attacks on merchant ships, two sunk, one seized, by late 2024
Many shipping lines rerouted around the Cape of Good Hope
Singapore to Rotterdam: about 15,300 km via Suez, about 21,800 km via the Cape, a difference of about 6,500 km
sources.source: Sea-distances port distance tables: 8,288 nm vs 11,755 nm (difference 3,467 nm, about 6,420 km, rounded to match the two rounded legs)

sources.claim: Egypt's president said the canal lost almost seven billion dollars in 2024
sources.source: President el-Sisi, 26 December 2024, reported by Reuters and AP ('almost $7 billion')

sources.claim: The US launched a naval coalition in December 2023
sources.source: US Department of Defense, Operation Prosperity Guardian, 18 December 2023

sources.claim: US and British strikes on Houthi targets began in January 2024; EU escorts began in February 2024
sources.source: US DoD and UK MoD, 12 January 2024; Council of the EU, Operation Aspides, 19 February 2024

sources.claim: The Houthis say they act in solidarity with Gaza and will stop when the war there does
sources.source: Houthi statements reported by Reuters, November 2023 to January 2025

sources.claim: The Houthis paused attacks during the January 2025 Gaza ceasefire
UN Security Council resolution 2722 demanded the Houthis stop attacks on merchant ships
Shipping groups said many targeted ships had no clear link to Israel and crews came from many countries
sources.source: International Chamber of Shipping and BIMCO statements, 2024

sources.claim: The Rubymar, carrying fertiliser, sank in March 2024
Oman announced a US-Houthi truce in May 2025; the Houthis said Israel was not included
Magic Seas and Eternity C sunk off Yemen in July 2025
After the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire attacks largely paused; shipping lines said any return would be gradual
The canal earned a record 10.25 billion dollars in 2023
sources.source: Suez Canal Authority, reported by Reuters, January 2024

sources.claim: The East-West pipeline to Yanbu can carry up to 7 million barrels a day
India, Saudi Arabia, the US, the EU and others signed plans for a corridor across Arabia in 2023; it is not yet built
sources.source: White House fact sheet, IMEC memorandum, 9 September 2023

sources.claim: Ethiopia signed a deal with Somaliland in January 2024 seeking coast; Ethiopia says it needs sea access
sources.source: Reuters, 1 January 2024; Reuters, October 2023 (PM Abiy speech)

sources.claim: Somalia called the deal a breach of its sovereignty
In December 2024 Ethiopia and Somalia agreed a path to settle the dispute in Turkey-brokered talks in Ankara
Assab is less than 100 km from Ethiopia's border; Eritrea says it will not discuss its coast
sources.source: Map measure; Eritrea Ministry of Information statement, October 2023, via Reuters

sources.claim: The attacks that turned ships away were launched from Yemen
sources.source: UN Security Council resolution 2722 (10 January 2024); US DoD statements 2024; AP tally, December 2024

sources.claim: Malacca carries much of Asia's oil
